The challenge is deciding how long exceptional growth and profitability can persist. Reported earnings can also include investment gains that do not measure recurring product economics. The strongest business case is that software, system integration and continued product leadership preserve exceptional profit conversion. The constraint is that research, transitions between products, supply requirements and competition remain real costs. Evidence of recurring net earnings through several product generations would support the mature assumption more strongly than a single quarter. Nvidia invented the GPU, the chip behind nearly every major AI system on the planet. But it’s so much more today. It sells entire “AI factories” in a box: multi-rack systems packed with processors, memory, servers, cooling, and the high-speed networking that lets everything work together like one big “brain.” And its CUDA software is so deeply embedded across every cloud, AI lab, and frontier model that it’s become the de facto AI infrastructure operating system. Nvidia grew revenue 106% year over year from $46.7 billion to $96.2 billion in fiscal Q2 2027 (ended July 26, 2026). That’s unprecedented. No public company in history has ever organically doubled quarterly revenue from such a large base. Nvidia’s “Data Center” revenue, which is the AI business, grew 117% year over year in Q2 to $89 billion. The company guided for total revenue of $108 billion this quarter, which would be its first $100 billion quarter. It also guided for 70% revenue growth in fiscal 2028, which is basically calendar year 2027. And the cap on that growth guidance is supply, not demand. The company said it would have been about double again absent the supply crunch. Meanwhile, the customer list has broadened considerably. For two years, the most popular argument against Nvidia was basically: “Its whole business depends on four giant customers, all of which are building their own chips to become less reliant on Nvidia.” It’s true that these four “hyperscalers”—Amazon, Microsoft, Google (GOOGL), and Meta Platforms (META)—have been driving much of the AI infrastructure buildout. They’ll continue to do so for at least a few more years. And all four are indeed building their own AI chips these days. But as the hyperscalers have increased their AI spending, so have lots of other companies. Governments around the world have too for their “sovereign AI” initiatives. And we now have a lot more color on that broadening AI spending… In Q1, Nvidia started separating its AI revenue into two buckets. Bucket one is the hyperscalers. Bucket two is everybody else, which Nvidia calls ACIE (short for AI Clouds, Industrial, and Enterprise). So ACIE covers the neoclouds, governments, hospitals, banks, carmakers, drug companies, AI startups, etc. Meanwhile, most of the customers in the faster-growing ACIE bucket will never even think about designing their own chips. What’s more, the hyperscalers have shown no signs of pulling back yet. Nvidia CFO Colette Kress said it clearly on the call: “With cloud industry backlog now greater than $2 trillion, CapEx by the top five hyperscalers is expected to reach nearly $800 billion in 2026 and $1.3 trillion in 2027.” (Oracle is the fifth hyperscaler she referred to.) And Amazon—which does design its own AI chips and has basically been Exhibit A for the whole “hyperscalers will defect” thesis—committed to deploying another 2 million Nvidia GPUs through 2028. Amazon is also adopting Nvidia’s full physical AI stack (Omniverse, Cosmos, Isaac, and Jetson) to power its fleet of warehouse robots. So the giants are still buying from Nvidia, a new class of customer has shown up behind them, and both are compounding at once. First, the Vera Rubin ramp. Nvidia expects supply to stay tight through at least fiscal 2028 (basically calendar 2027). We want to see the company deliver at least the 70% growth it expects. I also want gross margin to bottom in the 71% to 72% range. If it falls below that threshold, it means memory costs are temporarily winning the tug-of-war Second, how much Nvidia invests in, guarantees, and backstops its customers. It has about $165 billion in these types of financing arrangements. Critics call this “circular financing.” But we’re not concerned. Those guarantees are only about 1.3X Nvidia’s trailing 12-month free cash flow… and only about half of our two-year forward annual free cash flow forecast. What’s more, if a customer fails, what’s left behind is Nvidia equipment that other buyers are lining up for, not dark fiber like after the dot-com bust. Third, the Open Agent Safety Platform Nvidia launched just this week. It’s a two-piece (hardware and software) system for keeping AI agents inside the boundaries set by operators. The launch follows disclosures from OpenAI, Anthropic, Meta, and Google of recent incidents in which their AI models escaped their test sandboxes—during testing with safeguards reduced, I should add—and hacked other organizations. Nvidia says that from what it knows about the most notorious of such incidents—OpenAI’s models breaching Hugging Face—this new platform could have stopped it. The significance: Nvidia is basically trying to make its hardware the place where AI agent safety lives. And it’s giving away the software layer to make that architecture the industry default—the classic CUDA-style playbook applied to safety. It strengthens the “you need the whole Nvidia stack” narrative and gives CEO Jensen Huang a powerful talking point and a place at the table on one of the industry’s biggest problems. But it’s effectively an “option” on the future, not a moat today. And the open design means the door is deliberately left open for others. P.S. Nvidia (NVDA) is on track for its fifth straight losing week, and the slide since its October record has now erased nearly $1.4 trillion in market value. Thursday did a lot of the damage. Nvidia closed down more than 9%, knocking nearly $450 billion off its market value in a single session and leaving the company worth about $4.4 trillion. It was the stock's worst day since the DeepSeek sell-off in January 2025. AMD (AMD), Micron (MU), and Arm (ARM) suffered steep double-digit losses, and Broadcom (AVGO) and Taiwan Semiconductor (TSM) fell more than 10%. The PHLX Semiconductor Index (^SOX) had its worst day since March 2020 and is now more than a third below its June record. Sandisk (SNDK) dropped 22%. This price reflects trading activity during the overnight session on the Blue Ocean ATS, available 8 PM to 4 AM ET, Sunday through Thursday, when regular markets are closed. Nvidia itself is now about 24% below its Oct. 6 record close and trading below its 200-day moving average. The trigger this time is Washington. Democrats won both chambers of Congress, and candidates in both parties campaigned against AI data centers, the buildings that run on Nvidia's chips. The Senate came close to passing a bill this fall that would have made data centers pay more of the power costs they create. Losing streaks this long don't come often for Nvidia. Since its 1999 IPO, the stock has strung together five or more down weeks just 12 times before this one. The longest ran seven weeks, in the summer of 2008. The last one is the streak bulls will want to remember. It ended in October 2022, about a month before ChatGPT's launch set off the AI boom, and Nvidia's stock roughly quadrupled over the following year. That's the best case, not the base case. Nvidia was higher 13 weeks later in only five of the 12 earlier streaks, though it was up a year later in eight. The worst came in 2002, when the stock lost nearly two-thirds of its value over the following year. For now, Washington is the new worry hanging over the stock. title: NVDA Stock Faces the Last Support as Midterm Elections Put Data-Centre Spending and Nvidia Under Pressure - FXLeaders
content: Nvidia (NASDAQ: NVDA) stock has fallen below $200 to around $181, extending their retreat from record highs above $243 as Democratic victories in the US midterm elections intensify concerns about data-centre expansion, electricity shortages, financing costs and growing political opposition to the technology infrastructure boom. Nvidia shares have suffered another sharp reversal after failing to sustain their recover. The stock initially rebounded towards $210 last week, supported by improving geopolitical sentiment, but renewed selling pressure has pushed shares down to approximately $181. The latest decline reflects growing concerns about the enormous infrastructure commitments underpinning semiconductor valuations. Investors are increasingly questioning whether technology companies can maintain their current investment pace as financing costs rise, electricity availability becomes more challenging and political resistance to new data centers gains momentum. Nvidia has now retreated significantly from its record above $243, with the immediate technical picture deteriorating. The $180 area is the next important support zone, while a decisive break lower could expose further downside towards $150. Buyers would need to reclaim $200 to improve the immediate outlook and restore confidence in a recovery. The Democratic victories in the US midterm elections have introduced a new political risk for Nvidia and the wider semiconductor industry. Gina Hinojosa defeated incumbent Greg Abbott in Texas, becoming the state’s first Democratic governor in more than three decades. Her campaign included a proposal for an immediate freeze on new data-centre developments. Similar opposition has emerged in Ohio and Georgia, where Governor-elect Amy Acton and Governor-elect Keisha Lance Bottoms have also called for greater restrictions on unchecked infrastructure expansion. The election results highlight a broader shift in public sentiment. Reports indicate that 40 of 41 direct votes concerning data-centre projects failed, while several candidates supporting rapid expansion also lost their races. This creates a difficult environment for technology companies that have committed enormous amounts of capital to infrastructure construction. There are several reasons why investors are reassessing the sector: Political opposition: Local communities are increasingly resisting new data centres because of concerns about electricity consumption, water requirements and the impact on household utility bills. Electricity shortages: Power infrastructure may struggle to accommodate the pace of planned construction, potentially delaying projects and reducing the returns on invested capital. Higher construction costs: Companies could be forced to finance additional electricity generation and supporting infrastructure rather than relying entirely on existing power grids. Spending discipline: Investors are beginning to reward technology companies that demonstrate greater capital discipline rather than simply increasing infrastructure budgets. For Nvidia, this is particularly important because its future revenue expectations remain heavily dependent on continued spending by major cloud providers. NVIDIA shares lost momentum early in September after failing to break decisively above the $236 resistance zone, with the rejection sending the stock back below $210 but we have seen a decent rebound recently. Shares have climbed above $233 today as investors responded positively to expanding infrastructure partnerships and CEO projections, but buyers are not able to sustain the rally above $243 and we saw dive to $180 today where NVDA is testing the last support at the 100 weekly SMA in yellow. Despite the deteriorating share price, Nvidia continues to expand its influence across the semiconductor supply chain. CEO Jensen Huang’s reported involvement in Marvell Technology’s acquisition of Lumentum Holdings highlights the company’s strategic relationships with infrastructure suppliers. According to Bloomberg, Marvell CEO Matthew Murphy and Lumentum CEO Michael Hurlston consulted Huang before announcing the transaction, which values Lumentum at approximately $115 billion in enterprise value. Nvidia previously invested $2 billion in each company, strengthening its exposure to optical networking and data-centre connectivity. However, the enormous transaction also highlights the capital requirements associated with expanding the infrastructure supporting advanced computing. Not all developments point towards a slowdown. Reports indicate that Anthropic plans to increase its computing capacity beyond 3.5 gigawatts by the end of 2026, potentially reaching approximately 7 gigawatts in 2027. This demonstrates that demand for computing infrastructure remains substantial, providing support for Nvidia’s longer-term growth prospects. Samsung Electronics is also reportedly preparing to manufacture base dies for high-bandwidth memory chips intended for Nvidia and AMD at its second foundry facility in Taylor, Texas. Construction is expected to begin this month, with mass production targeted for 2030. Nevertheless, strong demand projections do not necessarily guarantee that infrastructure projects will be completed on schedule or generate sufficient returns. Competition is another challenge for Nvidia. Google and Oracle have announced plans to make Google’s Tensor Processing Units (TPUs) available through Oracle Cloud Infrastructure from 2027. This provides customers with another alternative to Nvidia-powered systems as major technology companies attempt to reduce computing costs and dependence on external suppliers. Nvidia maintains considerable advantages through its established software ecosystem, performance and customer relationships. However, the expansion of custom processors could eventually pressure pricing and market share, even if overall computing demand continues growing. Financing conditions are becoming increasingly important for the semiconductor industry. CoreWeave has experienced significant pressure as yields on its debt maturing in 2032 climbed towards 15%, highlighting the risks associated with heavily leveraged infrastructure expansion. Electricity shortages are also creating deployment problems. Amazon reportedly has Nvidia-equipped server racks waiting in warehouses because some data centres lack sufficient electricity to operate them. Such delays could increase storage costs and postpone revenue generation from infrastructure investments, raising further questions about the returns expected from the current spending cycle. Nvidia remains one of the strongest companies in the semiconductor industry, with substantial customer relationships and exposure to long-term computing demand. However, the market is increasingly questioning whether infrastructure spending can continue expanding at the pace previously anticipated. The Democratic election victories have brought political opposition to data-centre construction into the mainstream, adding to concerns about electricity availability, financing costs and competition. Technically, the decline below $200 represents a significant setback. The $180 level is now critical, with a sustained break potentially opening the door towards $150. A recovery above $200 would be needed to improve the immediate technical picture. For now, sellers remain in control. Despite continued demand for advanced processors, Nvidia shares could remain under pressure as investors demand stronger evidence that the enormous infrastructure investments supporting current valuations will generate sustainable returns.

Investing.com -- Chinese artificial intelligence startup Moonshot AI has explored leasing data center capacity in Europe to secure remote access to NVIDIA Corporation's (NASDAQ:NVDA) advanced Blackwell processors, according to a report from CNBC. The move highlights how Chinese developers are increasingly looking beyond domestic borders to bypass tightening U.S. export restrictions on cutting-edge silicon. The Beijing-based lab, known for its Kimi model family, discussed renting infrastructure from European neocloud providers hosting clusters of 8,000 or more Blackwell GPUs, CNBC reported, citing people familiar with the matter. Those discussions focused primarily on computing clusters for model inference, though interest in training capacity was also explored. The European push follows White House claims in July that Moonshot had remotely tapped Blackwell systems through infrastructure located in Thailand. While existing U.S. export controls forbid physical shipments of top-tier accelerators directly to China, current trade frameworks leave cross-border cloud leasing largely outside regulatory reach. To compensate for regulatory risks, European cloud operators and financiers have sought substantial upfront premiums, with proposals requiring Moonshot to pay 30% to 50% more upfront than non-Chinese clients, according to CNBC's reporting. The steeper initial deposits allow operators to front-load contract returns should Western regulators eventually close overseas cloud loopholes. Washington has already moved to address the arrangement, with the U.S. House of Representatives passing the Remote Access Security Act in January to restrict foreign cloud-based access to restricted hardware. The legislative effort now awaits action in the Senate, underscoring rising political scrutiny around third-party compute hosting. For its part, Nvidia has sought to manage geopolitical exposures by instructing cloud partners to allocate at least 51% of their capacity to non-Chinese customers, according to earlier reporting from the Financial Times. The chipmaker has defended its international footprint, arguing that widespread adoption of American hardware architectures remains critical to sustaining leadership across global software and model layers. Meanwhile, Moonshot's aggressive hunt for compute comes amid rapid enterprise adoption of lower-cost Chinese foundational models that rival Western leaders such as OpenAI and Anthropic. With Beijing simultaneously curbing domestic purchases of older, licensed Nvidia hardware to favor local silicon, China's leading AI labs are likely to remain reliant on creative offshore infrastructure arrangements to maintain model performance. The semiconductor industry has been supercharged in recent years by the rise and rapid adoption of artificial intelligence (AI), which isn't surprising, as chips are essential for running AI applications in data centers, smartphones, computers, vehicles, robots, and factories. Nvidia (NVDA -9.26%) and Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing (TSM -10.78%) are two of the most important players in the semiconductor space, which explains why they have been among the biggest beneficiaries of the AI-fueled semiconductor boom. Let's see why these semiconductor stocks will continue capitalizing on the AI chip market's growth, and which one is the better buy for the long run. Nvidia's dominant position in the graphics processing unit (GPU) space allowed it to quickly capitalize on the booming demand for AI chips, which were primarily used for training large language models (LLMs) during the initial phases of the AI rollout. Popular AI models, such as ChatGPT, Grok, Qwen, and others, have been trained using Nvidia's chips. The chip giant is now dominating the inference space as well, with a market share of more than 70%. This is great news for Nvidia investors, as AI compute is now shifting from training to inference. In fact, inference is expected to generate more revenue than training-oriented workloads in 2026, according to the Futurum Group. At the same time, the emergence of new AI niches will expand Nvidia's addressable market. Physical AI, for example, is expected to grow substantially over the long run. Physical AI refers to the integration of AI into objects that can be deployed in the real world, such as humanoid robots, autonomous vehicles, drones, and factory robots. Mordor Intelligence predicts that the physical AI market could clock annual growth of 37% through 2031. This expansion of AI beyond data centers should ensure that Nvidia's healthy growth continues. Not surprisingly, analysts expect Nvidia's earnings to more than double in just two fiscal years, and the long-term earnings per share (EPS) growth estimate of 50% (per YCharts) suggests it can sustain its momentum for a long time. Somebody is going to make a fortune on Anthropic’s IPO. It probably won’t be regular investors waiting for the day it goes public. Unless investors know where to look. Because two companies anyone can buy today already own pieces of Anthropic. And one of them owns a piece of OpenAI, too. Meanwhile, TSMC has been riding Nvidia's coattails by virtue of being the latter's foundry partner. Nvidia is a fabless chipmaker that utilizes TSMC's semiconductor manufacturing and packaging services to bring its chip designs into the physical form. However, the good part about TSMC is that it manufactures chips for multiple customers, including Apple, Sony, MediaTek, Broadcom, Marvell, and others. TSMC's broad customer base allows it to serve multiple AI-focused end markets, including smartphones, personal computers, robots, and data centers. So, TSMC seems better-positioned to capitalize on the semiconductor industry's long-term growth, which will be primarily fueled by AI. Industry association SEMI estimates that the global semiconductor industry's revenue reached $1 trillion in the first eight months of 2026. McKinsey expects the industry to generate $2.3 trillion in revenue in 2030. TSMC's status as the world's leading third-party chip manufacturer with a 73% market share, according to Counterpoint Research, makes it one of the best ways to play this lucrative space. Also, TSMC's dominant share explains why it is the price maker, meaning its price hikes are likely to be accepted by customers, including Nvidia. A recent report from Taiwan-based financial newspaper Commercial Times notes that TSMC could increase advanced chip packaging prices by up to 20%. So, I won't be surprised to see TSMC's margins heading higher in the future following an impressive jump this year. Both Nvidia and TSMC can deliver robust long-term growth. In fact, as the following chart tells us, there isn't much difference in the potential long-term EPS growth both companies are anticipated to deliver. That's why we will look at their valuations to determine which AI stock you should consider buying right now. So, TSMC and Nvidia are closely matched on the valuation front as well. Also, we have seen that both companies are projected to achieve nearly identical earnings growth over the long run. So, investors can consider buying either of these semiconductor stocks to capitalize on the AI infrastructure boom. Both companies dominate their respective niches in chip designing and manufacturing, which is why they are likely to grow at solid rates in the long run. Moreover, TSMC and Nvidia are attractively valued despite their healthy growth rates. The tech-laden Nasdaq Composite index, for comparison, has a price-to-earnings ratio of 40. So, investors are getting a solid deal on these semiconductor stocks, and buying either of them could prove to be a profitable long-term move for the reasons discussed in this article. title: Is The Nasdaq Selloff 2000 Or 2018? - Trefis
content: Follow the whole story: every piece in this series is on our AI storyline page. The Nasdaq 100 closed Monday more than 10% below its Oct 6 record. It gained 0.7% on Tuesday, when chip stocks bounced after three losing sessions, and 0.9% on Wednesday, ending about 9% below the record. The debate is the same one every correction brings: is this a bubble bursting, or a pullback in a bull market? The two cases are very different. From March 2000 to October 2002, the Nasdaq 100 lost about 83%. To get back to even from there takes a gain of almost 500%. In late 2018, the Nasdaq fell about 24% from its late-August high to Christmas Eve, then regained it within about four months. Two of three numbers say correction. The third says the risk is growing. 2000 forward P/Es are as of March 2000 for the seven largest companies at the time, from a Goldman Sachs comparison as reported in the press (median about 52; Cisco about 102, Oracle about 85, Microsoft about 53, Intel about 42). Published estimates of the Nasdaq 100’s forward P/E this year range from the low 20s to the high 20s; we haven’t measured it. The $1.15 is the four cloud giants’ Q3 2026 capex (about $202 billion) divided by their operating cash flow (about $175 billion), our estimate from reported figures; the full calculation is in our piece on why nobody stops spending on AI, the first question listed at the end. No. In March 2000, investors paid a median of about 52 times next year’s expected earnings for the seven largest companies, and more than 100 times for Cisco, then the most valuable company in the world. This year, published estimates put the whole Nasdaq 100 somewhere in the 20s times forward earnings. That’s expensive by history. But it’s about half of 2000, or less. Score: 2018-like. This is the biggest difference. Many 2000 Nasdaq companies had little or no profit. Even Cisco, the profitable leader, earned about $2.7 billion in its 2000 fiscal year while worth more than $500 billion at the peak. Today’s leaders are among the most profitable companies ever built. Microsoft brought in $58 billion of operating cash in the quarter ended September, up 29% from a year ago. Alphabet earned about $26 billion of profit in the same quarter. Azure grew 48% and AWS 39%. When prices fall on companies earning that much, the earnings give investors something solid to value, which 2000’s leaders didn’t have. Score: 2018-like. Here’s the number that doesn’t fit the comfortable story. In 2000, the build-out of the internet was paid for largely with borrowed money. When the money stopped, the builders went bust and their suppliers’ orders vanished. Today the four cloud giants mostly pay with their own cash, though Amazon and Alphabet together borrowed a net $74 billion in the third quarter. In that quarter, their capital spending ran about 15% ahead of the cash their businesses brought in. A year ago it was well under that line. And the companies that don’t have that cash are already borrowing heavily. Oracle had about $125 billion of borrowings at the end of August, plus another $288 billion of data-center leases that haven’t started yet. CoreWeave carried $35.6 billion of debt at midyear and holds a junk rating. The market has already drawn the line. Over the last 12 months, Oracle is down 50% and CoreWeave 58%, while Microsoft is up 8%. The debt-funded edge of AI is in its own 2000. The cash-funded center is not, yet. Score: mixed, moving toward 2000. If you can’t tell which year it is, size from the worse one. The idea is simple: decide the most you could lose on your AI holdings without changing your life or your plan, then work backward from the 2000 case, not the 2018 one. An example. Say you have $1 million invested and could live with losing $150,000 on the AI part. In a 2018-style drop of about 25%, you could hold $600,000 of AI stocks. In a 2000-style drop of about 75%, you could hold only $200,000. That $400,000 gap is the price of not knowing. Sizing for 2000 means you won’t be forced to sell at the bottom if it turns out to be 2000, and you still own a meaningful stake if it’s 2018. And watch the funding number every quarter. If the four giants come to finance the build-out mainly with bonds rather than cash, the scorecard flips to 2000 on the third count, and it’s time to revisit your size. Know the worst case before you need it. The worst case isn’t volatility; it’s the specific loss you’d live through, and how long it lasts. For the Nasdaq 100 that history is a fall of 83% and a recovery measured in years. You don’t need to believe it will happen to plan for it. You only need to make sure that if it does, you don’t have to sell. On valuation and profits, this is 2018. On funding, it is drifting toward 2000. Today’s leaders cost about half of what 2000’s did, or less, and earn vastly more. But they now spend more than they bring in, and the debt-funded builders are already down 50% to 58%. Size your AI holdings for the 2000 case, buy any further drop at prices you set, and recheck the funding number each quarter. We’ll rescore these three numbers after every quarter’s earnings. Follow the story, and send us the number you’d add to the scorecard. Corrections test concentration, not conviction. title: Nvidia Stock To $129? - Trefis
content: Part of our AI selloff guide. Start here: what the Nasdaq correction means for your money. Follow the whole story: every piece in this series is on our AI storyline page. The Nasdaq 100 closed Monday more than 10% below its Oct 6 peak, which is the textbook definition of a correction. The worst day was Friday, Oct 30, when chip stocks (the iShares Semiconductor ETF) fell about 8% after Amazon’s and Alphabet’s results and a weak profit forecast from Intel. By Wednesday the index had bounced to about 9% below its peak, but chip stocks fell another 3% that day. The fear behind the selloff is simple: JPMorgan expects about $900 billion of AI spending worldwide in 2026, and investors want to know when that money pays back. The stock at the center of AI spending is down the least. The deepest falls are company-specific or come after the biggest run-ups. If this were purely a vote against AI spending, Nvidia, the biggest chip company and the one most tied to that spending, should be leading the way down. It isn’t. Intel lost more than a third of its value in five days after its own forecast. Micron and Dell are down hard, but both had more than doubled over the past year. 12-month price changes to Nov 4: Micron +265%, Dell +141%, AMD +95%, Marvell +82%, Intel +57%, Nvidia +1%, Broadcom −8%, Super Micro −38%. Prices are the Wed Nov 4 close (Trefis market data). AMD closed Tue Nov 3, before its report, at $483.90. “Below 52-week high” is how far each stock sits under its highest close of the past year. A stock that more than doubled can fall 30% and still be up on the year; Micron is the clearest case. Company-specific. Intel fell on its own weak profit forecast, not on anyone’s AI budget. Its 39% five-day drop is the biggest in the table. Super Micro has been falling for a year (−38% over 12 months) for reasons that started before this selloff. The payoff doubt. Memory (Micron), networking and optical chips (Marvell) and the companies that build AI servers (Dell, Super Micro) all sold off together after the big cloud companies reported. These businesses get paid first when data centers are built, so they’re the first to be marked down when investors worry that building slows. Marvell’s 36% five-day drop is the biggest of that group. Nvidia and Broadcom sit in between. They are the biggest chip companies selling into AI spending, but they’ve held up best over the past five days (−7% each). That tells you the market isn’t yet betting that the spending stops. It’s betting that the spending gets more careful, and that the suppliers with the thinnest edge get squeezed first. A lot further than this, usually. From late 2021 to late 2022, chip stocks (the iShares Semiconductor ETF) fell about 46% from their peak, and Nvidia fell about 66%. In late 2018, Nvidia lost more than half its value in about three months. In the 2000–2002 bust, many chip stocks fell by more than 80%: Intel about 82%, AMD about 93%. And it’s not only chips: Meta fell about 77% from its 2021 peak to its 2022 low, and it stayed profitable throughout. Here’s what a 2022-sized fall (46% from the 52-week high) would mean for each stock today: The 52-week highs are each stock’s highest close of the past year. For Nvidia, a repeat of its own 2022 fall (−66%) would mean about $81 a share. That’s the outer edge, not a forecast. In 2022, the Fed was raising interest rates fast, from near zero to above 4%. That isn’t the main story today. Here’s what this table means at home: if you own broad index funds, you own every one of these stocks, often on top of the ones you bought yourself. Chip stocks have fallen 46% to 66% before, in less than a year. If you have $1 million or more invested, a Trefis partner firm can show you how much of your portfolio rides on one industry. That the slowdown investors fear hasn’t reached AMD’s order book. It reported after the close on Tuesday, Nov 3: third-quarter revenue of $13.4 billion, up 45%, against about $13.1 billion expected, and record data center revenue of $8.5 billion, up 97%. The number that mattered was the fourth-quarter guide: about $17 billion, plus or minus 3%, against the roughly $16.3 billion analysts expected. CEO Lisa Su added that she expects revenue to grow more than 80% in 2027. AMD closed Tuesday at $483.90, before the report, 25% below its 52-week high. After rising more than 4% in early trading Wednesday, it closed up only 1.0%, at $488.78, while Nvidia fell 3.2%. The market took it as good news for AMD, not yet as an all-clear for the group: AMD can grow by taking share even if total AI spending slows, and Nvidia, already far bigger than AMD, has less room to do that. What AMD’s guidance says about the slide, and whether the drop was overdone. Nvidia reports on Tuesday, Nov 17. It guided this quarter’s revenue to about $108 billion, plus or minus 2%. Nvidia is the real test of the payoff question because its customers are the companies doing much of that $900 billion of spending. If its outlook for next quarter keeps rising, the selloff in suppliers looks like a scare. If it flattens, the 2022 yardstick starts to apply to Nvidia too. Two of the eight have already fallen as far as chip stocks did in 2022; Nvidia has fallen about a third of that far. The worst drops of the past five days are Intel’s own forecast and a reset in the suppliers that had run furthest. AMD’s beat-and-raise on Tuesday says its customers are still buying; whether the whole group avoids a 2022-style reset now rides on Nvidia’s report in about two weeks. It’s how much a full-blown drop would take from you, in dollars. Here is the math for a $5 million portfolio with $2 million, 40%, in AI megacaps. In a 2022-style drop, the 40% in AI stocks causes two-thirds of the loss. The same $5 million held entirely in the “everything else” mix would have lost about $800,000 in the 2022-style case and $750,000 in the 2000-style one. Their peak-to-bottom falls in 2021–22 were about −66%, −37%, −44%, −56%, −77% and −31%, an average near −52%; we use −50% because the peaks and bottoms didn’t all land on the same days. “Everything else” is a 60/40-style mix of stocks and bonds, which lost about 16% in calendar 2022 because bonds fell too. In the 2000 bust the Nasdaq 100 fell about 83%; leaders such as Cisco, Intel and Oracle fell 80% or more, Microsoft about 65%. We use −75% for the megacaps, a bit less than 2000’s leaders fell, because today’s leaders are already highly profitable, and −15% for the rest because bonds rose in 2000–02 while stocks fell. Wednesday’s snapshot: Nvidia 16% below its 52-week high, Alphabet 28%, Meta 19%, Amazon 6%; Microsoft and Apple closed at 52-week highs. They already have. From their 2021 peaks to their 2022 lows, Meta lost about 77% and Alphabet about 44%. Those weren’t failing companies. Both were back to record profits by 2024. Their stocks fell as rates rose and investors stopped paying any price for growth. Today’s version of that worry is whether roughly $900 billion of AI spending worldwide this year (JPMorgan’s estimate) earns its money back. Alphabet and Meta are among the ones writing those checks, and they’re down 16% and 13% this month while Apple is up 5%. Because nobody decided it. Index funds add more of the same names: the biggest AI companies now make up a large share of the S&P 500 and an even larger share of the Nasdaq 100. If $2 million of stock cost $500,000, selling it all triggers a $1.5 million gain, about $357,000 in federal tax at the 23.8% top rate on long-term gains, before any state tax. That’s the real trade-off for most concentrated families: a tax bill you can see versus a drawdown you can’t. Watch the 30-day wash-sale rule if you plan to buy back. Sell in stages. Spreading sales over two or more tax years can keep more of the gain in lower brackets. Late December and early January are two tax years, a few weeks apart. Collar the position. Buying a put and selling a call puts a floor and a ceiling on a stock, often at little upfront cost. Collars that are too tight can count as a sale for tax purposes, so the structure matters. Exchange funds. They usually require a seven-year hold and are open only to wealthier investors. Give appreciated shares. content: Follow the whole story: every piece in this series is on our AI storyline page. The Nasdaq 100 fell about 1.4% on Monday and closed more than 10% below its Oct 6 peak, the line that marks a correction. It’s the index’s third correction this year, after March and July. By Wednesday’s close it had bounced to about 9% below the peak. Friday, Oct 30, was the worst day: the Nasdaq 100 fell about 3.5% and chip stocks (the iShares Semiconductor ETF) lost about 8% after Amazon’s and Alphabet’s results and a weak forecast from Intel. So the useful question isn’t “is the market down?” It’s “which part of the AI story did investors stop believing?” The selloff is aimed at the AI builders and the suppliers whose sales depend on them, not at big tech as a whole. Look at the bottom of the table. Apple and Microsoft, two of the three biggest companies in the world, are up this month and closed Wednesday at 52-week highs. The pain is concentrated in the companies whose next few years depend on AI spending continuing at today’s pace. Returns are to the close on Wed Nov 4, with the past month measured from the Oct 2 close (Trefis market data). “Below its 52-week high” uses the highest close of the past year. Intel’s month includes a one-day fall of about 29% after its forecast, its worst day in more than four decades. Others in the selloff: Dell −34%, Super Micro −32%, Micron −26%, Meta −13%, Palantir −9%, Broadcom −8% over the past month. Speculative AI-adjacent names fell harder: Cipher Mining −59%, Oklo −38%, Applied Digital −35%, IonQ −33%. Amazon rose 6% over the month. Not demand. After Monday’s close, Palantir reported a quarter with revenue up 96%, and the stock fell about 3.7% over the next two days, to $171.70. Amazon and Alphabet said last week that AI demand is still running ahead of the capacity they can install. What changed is the price investors will pay for that growth, because the bill has gotten very large. JPMorgan puts this year’s AI spending worldwide at about $900 billion, and $5.5 trillion in total through 2030. That spending is income for Nvidia, AMD and Marvell, and a cost for Alphabet, Meta and Oracle. When the spenders raise their budgets, investors now ask whether the payback is getting further away. When suppliers report, investors ask how long the budgets can keep growing. Either way, the stock falls. Add a 10-year Treasury yield near 4.9%, which makes profits far in the future worth less today, and you get a correction in exactly the stocks priced furthest into the future. Mostly well, but not always. Since 1985 the Nasdaq Composite has closed 10% or more below its record about 25 times, and 8 of those, roughly one in three, turned into bear markets of 20% or more. After the Nasdaq first closes in a correction, its median return over the next 12 months has been about +25%. The bad cases are the ones people remember: The pattern: drops caused by a shock from outside (Covid, tariffs, the Fed) healed in months. Drops that came after prices ran far ahead of profits, like 2000 and 2022, took years. This one is the second kind of question: it’s about whether AI spending pays. That doesn’t mean it ends like 2000. It means earnings, not headlines, will decide it. And even giants fall in that kind of market: from their 2021 peaks to their 2022 lows, Meta lost about 77% and Alphabet about 44%. Already in: AMD, Tuesday night (Nov 3). It beat, guided the fourth quarter above estimates and said it expects revenue to grow more than 80% in 2027. The stock closed up only 1% on Wednesday. Same day: the midterm elections, which matter less than you’d think. Jobs report, Fri Nov 6, and inflation, Tue Nov 10. With the 10-year near 4.9%, a hot number could push yields higher and hit the most expensive stocks again. Nvidia, Tue Nov 17. The biggest single test. Nvidia is the AI trade’s scoreboard: if its customers are still ordering at the same pace, the “is it paying off?” fear eases. Not broken, but repricing. AI demand is still growing; what broke is investors’ willingness to pay any price for it. History says about two in three Nasdaq corrections end before becoming bear markets. Whether this one does depends on Nvidia’s report on Nov 17, not on the headlines in between. A pullback that holds (about 55%). AMD has shown its orders are still there; if Nvidia does too, the index bottoms short of a 20% fall, as about two in three corrections have. A 2022-style bear market (about 35%). Yields stay near 5% and one or two big spenders trim their 2027 budgets. The index falls 25% to 35%, and the most-hyped names fall much further. Recovery takes a year or two. A 2000-style bust (about 10%). Spending is cut sharply, suppliers’ sales drop and the profits that today’s prices assume never arrive. Rare, and it needs both of the other paths’ triggers at once. title: NVDA, INTC Stocks Look Cheaper Than AMD Against Fair Value, Morningstar Says - Stocktwits
content: Morningstar believes that Nvidia (NVDA) and Intel (INTC) shares have more room to run than Advanced Micro Devices (AMD), despite a hike in the firm’s fair value estimate for the stock. Senior analyst Brian Colello raised his fair value estimate for AMD to $570 a share from $530, while maintaining a ‘fairly valued’ rating. Meanwhile, Nvidia and Intel retained their ‘undervalued’ ratings with price targets of $570 and $85, respectively. Morningstar’s fair value estimates imply a potential upside of around 50% for Nvidia, 40% for Intel, and 18% for AMD. In pre-market trading on Thursday, AMD stock fell as much as 2.6%, while NVDA edged 0.3% lower and INTC shares dropped 1.2%. The overall tech sector was weaker, with the Nasdaq-100 tracking Invesco QQQ Trust Series 1 (QQQ) falling around 1.6% in early morning trade. Colello said that the firm sees limits on AMD’s path against Nvidia. “AMD will need to improve its software capabilities to make a dent in Nvidia’s AI dominance, as Nvidia is strong in not only GPUs but also associated AI software tools,” he wrote. “AI offers a massive opportunity to GPU makers, and while AMD lags industry leader Nvidia, we see plenty of room in the AI market for AMD.” On Intel, Colello noted that the older chipmaker has not lost its footing in PCs. “Despite AMD’s recent share gains, Intel remains the industry leader in PC CPUs and might recapture most of the market if it can deliver industry-leading manufacturing capabilities once again,” he wrote. Morningstar’s higher valuation for AMD rests partly on the expected growth of its server CPU business. “We attribute our optimism to the rise of agentic AI, which should require exponentially more server CPUs for agentic orchestration workloads,” Collelo wrote. Morningstar also raised its expectations for AMD’s server processor business. “We’re more impressed with AMD’s commentary for 2027, as server CPU revenue should grow 100%-plus, above prior expectations of 70%-plus,” the analyst said. The firm expects AMD’s overall revenue to grow at a compound annual rate of 44% from 2026 to 2030. Its estimates also point to a sharp increase in AI GPU revenue, from $7.4 billion in 2025 to just under $17 billion in 2026, nearly $43 billion in 2027 and $80 billion by 2030. The forecast does not assume that growth will continue uninterrupted. Morningstar said it had built in a pause in demand, followed by a recovery. “We bake in a pause in demand at some point and assume only 5% growth in 2032, but nearly 10% of revenue growth per year thereafter as AMD cements its place as a prominent AI vendor,” Colello explained. The firm gave AMD a ‘Very High’ uncertainty rating. “AI is moving at warp speed, and future workloads and improvements are uncertain,” Colello said. AMD’s AI opportunity comes with risks in the PC segment, Morningstar said. It cited rising memory costs and concerns about PC demand in 2027. It pointed to Apple CEO John Ternus’ comments during the company’s fourth-quarter (Q4) earnings call on Monday. “What we’re seeing with memory pricing right now is unprecedented,” he said. Morningstar said it sees similar pressure building in the PC market. “High memory chip prices may stunt PC production and demand for AMD’s PC CPUs in 2027,” the firm wrote. Colello said his lower forecast for AMD’s client PC business was “consistent with the gloomy comments about the PC market made by rival Intel last week.” He expects the company’s data center business to help offset the slowdown. However, AMD might be less exposed to the pressure than Intel, according to Morningstar. Colello noted that AMD “has less PC exposure than Intel and believes it has more content in premium PCs that may be less price-sensitive to the high memory costs plaguing demand.” On Stocktwits, retail sentiment around AMD continued to trend in ‘extremely bullish’ territory, accompanied by ‘extremely high’ levels of chatter. Some retail traders on the platform applauded CEO Lisa Su’s confidence in a significant fourth-quarter ramp in Helios rack-scale AI system deployments. Others viewed AMD stock’s recent weakness as temporary noise that does not reflect the company’s underlying performance. Arthur Hayes expects "insiders unlock and dump" to flood SpaceX (SPCX) stock, then follow suit with Anthropic (ANT) and OpenAI (OPEAZZX), triggering a credit squeeze that ends in a central bank bailout that lifts crypto and makes Bitcoin (BTC) ‘glorious’ in the long run. Hayes made the case Thursday in a Substack essay called "D For Dilution." In his essay, he said the three companies' stocks would struggle as locked-up shares held by insiders become free to trade. Then falling share prices will make it harder for the companies to borrow, tightening the dollar liquidity crypto depends on, Hayes wrote. "This presents an issue for the general market environment because the entire AI trade rests on vibes. The vibes surrounding whether you believe the lofty future profitability and ubiquity of AI determine whether you lend money to the industry," Hayes added. Hayes compared the setup to Zcash (ZEC) back in 2016. Early adopters bought at high prices with a small amount of the token available, and most are still underwater even as Zcash's market value has grown since. You don't trade the market cap; you trade the price per token," he wrote. ZEC’s price was up over 2%, trading around $1,318. SpaceX's stock price has been relatively stable since its initial public offering, but the number of publicly traded shares has increased by about 50%, Hayes said. He projected that some 8.6 billion additional shares will be available by the end of June 2027. That would increase the float by roughly another 50%, mostly because of the vesting of the shares held by Elon Musk. The rumored combination of SpaceX and Tesla (TSLA) could mean about a 50% dilution for Class A shareholders, Hayes said. The stock can only be supported with an increase in free cash flow, Hayes said. He also said Musk would have to return that cash through dividends or buybacks. Anthropic filed its S-1, the registration statement a company submits to U.S. regulators before an IPO, in late October and intends to go public on Nasdaq under the ticker ANT. An AI agent looked at the filing on his behalf, Hayes said. There's no near-term dividend expectation, he said, and the company will plow its money into about $900 billion of compute commitments. Based on that schedule, Hayes wrote, "it is almost impossible mathematically for the stock price to go up between listing and June 2027." He figured that the selloff would take about $1.245 trillion in new money to absorb the price if Anthropic is valued at $1.5 trillion at market. Hayes also said investors should think of Anthropic as an oil and gas company rather than a software company, given customers pay for usage and past spending doesn't guarantee future demand. He noted reports that the company had cut its fundraising target from $30 billion to $20 billion and its valuation from $1.5 trillion to $1.25 trillion. Hayes believes a future OpenAI IPO would be structured similarly to SpaceX and Anthropic, with a small float and heavy insider sales in the months ahead. Companies can't borrow money in the debt markets on their own. They have to be publicly traded, Hayes said. If their shares fall, lenders will demand higher yields. That would eat into those loans, Hayes said, who said bank loans powered the crypto rally that began in August. Last week, the U.S. bank balance sheets contracted, we observed. "This is the transmission channel from AI to crypto." His family office, Maelstrom, will stay clear, said Hayes. He believes the central banks will print money once the AI slump turns into a crisis threat. That, he said, "will be glorious for Bitcoin and crypto holders. But be patient." AMC Entertainment Holdings (AMC) stock is heading for its best weekly gain since July, after the theater chain posted record third-quarter (Q3) revenue and Adjusted EBITDA, and CEO Adam Aron declared on X that AMC “has recovered”—a stock attempting to claw back four years of losses. AMC Entertainment stock traded over 2% lower overnight, ahead of Thursday. The stock has gained 15% so far this week and is on track to reverse four years of losses. The rally tests whether a record quarter can change how Wall Street prices a company that spent years as a survival story. AMC still reported a nine-month GAAP net loss, and its stock trades at a valuation unlike its peers’. Aron is betting that a $10 billion-plus box office makes the old debt and dilution worries obsolete. For the better part of four years, AMC Entertainment’s story was about staying alive. This week, its CEO argued that story is over. “Today, we can finally say that AMC has recovered,” Aron posted on X after the company reported Q3 results on Wednesday. He called the quarter “a triumph” and said AMC’s biggest and best in its 106-year history. The numbers back him on growth. Q3 revenue rose 31.6% year-on-year to $1.711 billion, up from $1.300 billion last year. Adjusted EBITDA jumped 183.7% to $347.5 million, nearly triple last year’s figure. Adjusted EBITDA margin hit a record 20.3%, more than double the 9.4% from a year ago. It was the second straight quarter in which AMC set all-time company records for both revenue and Adjusted EBITDA. Analysts had expected about $1.62 billion in revenue and earnings of $0.10 a share, according to Fiscal.ai estimates cited by Stocktwits. AMC reported adjusted earnings of $0.13, against a loss of 58 cents a year ago. Operating cash flow was $176.6 million, versus a $14.9 million outflow a year ago. Free cash flow was $109.3 million, which brings the year-to-date total to $124.7 million. That is why Aron sees AMC posting positive free cash flow for all of 2026. Cash and equivalents more than doubled to $751.9 million, excluding $39.6 million in restricted cash. Attendance did the heavy lifting. Q3 attendance rose 28.3% to 74.9 million moviegoers, with international markets up 41.5% and U.S. markets up 23.3%. AMC did this with slightly fewer screens, averaging 9,177 versus 9,354 a year ago. The company also reported record revenue per patron, which Aron credited to its loyalty programs and its growing roster of premium large-format auditoriums. Aron also leaned on the balance sheet. On Oct. 5, AMC completed a $3.97 billion refinancing covering about 97% of its debt, pushing maturities out to late 2031 and 2033. During the Q3 earnings call, Aron addressed critics directly. He called any future article describing AMC as overly debt-laden “mindlessly in error.” He said “groundless fears of endless share dilution will come only from those looking in the rearview mirror.” He did not rule out new stock sales, saying AMC will “wisely utilize equity financings when it makes sense.” His argument rests on the macro backdrop. AMC now operates in a box office above $10 billion, he said, “a very different animal” from the $7 billion to $9 billion range of the past four years. Q4 looks strong so far. Aron said October’s domestic box office ran about 35% above the same month last year. The remaining slate includes The Hunger Games: Sunrise on the Reaping, Dune: Part Three, Avengers: Doomsday and Jumanji: Open World. He expects the domestic and global box office to reach their highest full-year levels in seven years. AMC has gained about 125% in 2026 as of late October, ahead of IMAX (IMAX), Cinemark (CNK) and streaming giant Netflix (NFLX). Even with record quarters, its first nine months produced a net loss of $19.2 million, or $0.03 share. Nine-month adjusted net earnings were a modest $26.9 million. Until GAAP profits become consistent, valuation arguments for AMC will rest on EBITDA and cash flow rather than earnings. The next few months will decide whether this week’s 15% gain is the start of a re-rating. The stock has registered a 192% increase in message volume over the past week. Another user said, “$109.3 million in quarterly free cash flow with expectation for positive free cash flow for all of 2026! Stay Zen AMC family. Our time will come.” AMC stock has gained 40% in the past twelve months. Read Next: Why Did AAPL, MSFT, AMC Stocks Surge To 52-Week Highs? Chip stocks plunged on Thursday, with Nvidia, Micron and AMD leading a sharp selloff that dragged the Nasdaq Composite down nearly 5% as investors reassessed the outlook for AI infrastructure spending and regulation. The Nasdaq fell 1,211 points, or 4.71%, putting it more than 10% below last month's record and into correction territory. The S&P 500 shed 245 points, or 3.19%, putting it on track for its worst session since April 2025, while the Dow Jones Industrial Average dropped 1,236 points, or 2.32%. More than $2 trillion was wiped from the US stock market within 50 minutes of the opening bell. Chipmakers bore the brunt of the selling. Nvidia Corp (NASDAQ:NVDA, XETRA:NVD) fell more than 6%, while Micron Technology Inc (NASDAQ:MU) dropped over 12% and Advanced Micro Devices Inc (NASDAQ:AMD, XETRA:AMD) lost more than 13%. The semiconductor index declined about 7%, while Broadcom Inc (NASDAQ:AVGO, XETRA:1YD) also fell 7%, Oracle Corp (NYSE:ORCL, XETRA:ORC) slipped close to 5% and Qualcomm Inc (NASDAQ:QCOM, XETRA:QCI) tumbled 9% after its outlook disappointed investors despite better-than-expected results. The selloff came as investors assessed what a Democratic sweep in the midterm elections could mean for AI infrastructure investment, particularly the construction of power-hungry data centers. Nigel Green, CEO of financial advisory group deVere Group, said the political shift was forcing markets to reconsider the costs and risks associated with the AI buildout. "Power, water, land and the cost of financing all of it via borrowing suddenly look less certain," Green said, adding that the repricing could take more than a few trading sessions. Democratic victories in the House and Senate, alongside key governorships, have raised concerns about potential restrictions on data center development and higher costs for electricity and water. Green said operators with heavy debt, thin margins and projects dependent on uncertain grid connections could face the greatest pressure. The rotation out of technology shares was accompanied by gains in defensive sectors, including healthcare, consumer staples and energy. Treasury prices also rose, pushing the 10-year yield down to 4.83%, while gold gained 0.9% to $4,098 an ounce. Green cautioned against treating the selloff as evidence that AI demand was disappearing, noting that companies with stronger balance sheets and established earnings could prove more resilient. However, he said volatility was likely to persist as investors reassessed the economics of AI investment and the potential impact of changing policies. Between October 6 and November 4, 2026, NVIDIA (NVDA) stock fell 16.3% while the S&P 500 lost 1.6%. Anyone thinking of buying wants to know whether that drop is a chance or a warning. The answer depends less on demand, which management says is larger than NVIDIA can supply, than on what meeting that demand will cost the company. First, how strong is NVIDIA's business right now? NVIDIA's Sales Growth Has Sped Up Four Quarters Running The latest results show a very strong business. Revenue rose 105.9% from a year earlier to $96.2 billion in fiscal Q2 2027, the quarter that ended July 26, 2026. Growth had been 62.5% in fiscal Q3 2026, and it accelerated in each quarter after that. That 62.5% was itself up from 55.6% in fiscal Q2 2026. NVIDIA also keeps an unusual share of its sales as profit. Its operating margin over the last twelve months was 65.2%, against 18.7% for the S&P 500. Investors pay 25.1 times NVIDIA's earnings over the last twelve months, against 22.8 for the S&P 500. A multiple only a little above the broader market reflects profits that more than doubled in a year. Net income over the last twelve months was $193 billion, against $86.6 billion a year earlier. If profits fell back, the same share price would mean a higher multiple. Management's own forecast indicates the next round will cost more than the last. On the August 26, 2026 call, management said memory prices had risen more than it expected and were still heading higher. Gross margin was 75% in fiscal Q2 2027, and the company expects 74%, plus or minus 50 basis points, in fiscal Q3. Management expects the margin to reach its low in fiscal Q4 at 71% to 72%. In fiscal 2028, it expects 72% to 73% as price increases NVIDIA has already made take effect. Management's account suggests demand is the smaller question. The company forecasts revenue of $108 billion, plus or minus 2%, for fiscal Q3 2027. For fiscal 2028, management expects growth of about 70%. It said customers' own forecasts point to faster growth than that, with supply holding NVIDIA back. NVIDIA is also using its own balance sheet to support some of that demand. Management said demand from AI labs it expects to back this way will make up roughly a quarter of its business in fiscal 2028, and that it will provide credit support for nearly 2 gigawatts of compute for one lab. Management said it knows some will call this circular financing, and that it sees the arrangement differently. In fiscal Q2 2027, NVIDIA's cash from operations was $24.1 billion, well below its net income of $59.7 billion. Management said inventory rose to $32 billion in the same quarter ahead of the Vera Rubin launch, and some large customers were given longer to pay. The stock has fallen further than the S&P 500 in four of five recent market shocks. In the 2025 US tariff shock, NVIDIA fell 32%, against 19% for the index. The 2023 regional banking crisis was the exception, when NVIDIA fell less than the index. The deepest fall came in the 2022 inflation shock and Fed tightening, when NVIDIA lost 63% against 24% for the S&P 500. You can hold through falls like these more easily if gross margin settles where management expects and the sales NVIDIA backs with its own balance sheet turn into cash. When NVIDIA reports in November 2026, gross margin against the guide management gave for fiscal Q3 2027 is the number to watch. title: Here's What $10,000 Invested in SpaceX and Nvidia Could Be Worth by 2030 - The Motley Fool
content: Space Exploration Technologies (SPCX -9.05%) and Nvidia (NVDA -9.26%) are two of the largest companies in the world. While they may seem unrelated, they're actually close partners, as SpaceX has a massive and growing artificial intelligence (AI) segment. In fact, it is planning to use Nvidia's latest-generation Vera Rubin processor architecture exclusively in its new data centers. SpaceX and Nvidia offer two completely different angles on AI investment: Nvidia is infrastructure, while SpaceX is application. Investing in both is a great way to get exposure to two of the primary facets of the AI trend. But what could a $10,000 investment split evenly between the two of them today be worth by 2030? Although AI has found its way into a wide array of use cases, the reality is there are a lot more out there. We've only seen the tip of the iceberg of what AI is capable of, and there still isn't enough computing capacity available to run all of the AI workloads that are popping up. As a result, there will be several more years of heavy AI infrastructure spending. This bodes well for Nvidia, as it means there will be several more years of strong demand for its GPUs. In fact, Nvidia projects that global data center capital expenditures will reach $3 trillion to $4 trillion by 2030. For reference, the big five AI hyperscalers are expected to spend nearly $800 billion on capex in 2026. So, even if we estimate that the entire world spent $1 trillion on data center capital expenditures this year, that forecast implies that total data center spending could rise threefold to fourfold over the next few years. One of those big spenders will be SpaceX. A few months before it went public, it bought another of CEO Elon Musk's companies: xAI. That acquisition has rapidly become a huge part of SpaceX's business. xAI trains and operates the Grok AI model, along with all its product offshoots (such as Grok Bots). Because SpaceX is on the application side of AI, its runway is practically unlimited. Moreover, business is good. In the third quarter, revenues from SpaceX's artificial intelligence segment, which it has renamed its "super intelligence" (SI) segment, soared 830% year over year. That shows just how quickly AI tools are being deployed, and the future looks bright for SpaceX. For Nvidia, projecting its rise is a bit clearer. If total AI spending in 2030 reaches the bottom end of its projection, don't be surprised to see Nvidia's business grow threefold as well. That would transform a $5,000 investment in Nvidia into $15,000 if the stock grows in parallel to the business (which it should over the long term). SpaceX is a bit trickier, as it couldn't sustain the rapid growth rate it achieved in Q3 for multiple years without its revenues getting absurdly large. However, CEO Elon Musk made the bold projection that SpaceX could have $500 billion to $1 trillion in annual recurring revenue by the end of next year, with its growth driven by the AI boom. Investors should take Musk's predictions with a grain of salt, but he's not wrong about the potential of AI and the rapid pace of its adoption. If we push that revenue prediction out to 2030, and settle at the bottom end of the range, it still points to impressive returns. If SpaceX can generate $500 billion in 2030 in revenue and if the stock trades then at 10 times sales, that would value the company at $5 trillion, up from around $1.8 trillion today. That would transform a $5,000 investment today into nearly $14,000. So a combined $10,000 investment in these two could yield about $29,000 by 2030. That's a great return in a short time frame, making these two AI stocks smart buys now. Keithen Drury has positions in Nvidia. The Motley Fool has positions in and recommends Nvidia. title: NVDA Stock Tests $200 Support as Political Backlash Hits Nvidia and Chip Sector - FXLeaders
content: Nvidia (NASDAQ: NVDA) stock has reversed below $200 as Democratic victories in the US midterm elections raise concerns about political opposition to data-centre expansion, while rising financing costs, infrastructure constraints and growing competition add pressure to the semiconductor sector. Nvidia shares have struggled to maintain their recovery after retreating from record highs above $243. The stock initially rebounded from the $200 level on Tuesday, climbing towards $210 as improving geopolitical sentiment provided some support for technology shares. However, the recovery quickly lost momentum as investors reassessed the sustainability of enormous infrastructure spending commitments. The latest Democratic election victories have added another challenge, sending chipmakers and companies connected to data-centre construction lower. Nvidia is particularly exposed to these developments because its growth expectations depend heavily on continued investment by major cloud providers and technology companies. The stock is now testing support around $200. A decisive break below this level could expose further downside towards $180, while buyers need to reclaim $210 to improve the immediate technical outlook. The political landscape has become increasingly important for Nvidia and the wider semiconductor industry. Democratic victories in several key states have strengthened opposition to rapid data-centre expansion, particularly in Texas. Gina Hinojosa defeated incumbent Greg Abbott, becoming Texas’s first Democratic governor in more than three decades. During her campaign, Hinojosa advocated an immediate freeze on new data-centre developments. Similar concerns are emerging in Ohio and Georgia, where Governor-elect Amy Acton and Governor-elect Keisha Lance Bottoms have also campaigned against unchecked digital infrastructure growth. These developments do not necessarily mean existing projects will be cancelled, but tighter permitting requirements, electricity restrictions and construction delays could complicate future expansion. For Nvidia, the concern is that political resistance could eventually affect the pace of infrastructure investment and demand for its advanced processors. Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang’s reported involvement in Marvell Technology’s acquisition of Lumentum Holdings highlights the company’s growing influence across the semiconductor supply chain. According to Bloomberg, Marvell CEO Matthew Murphy and Lumentum CEO Michael Hurlston consulted Huang before announcing the transaction, which values Lumentum at approximately $115 billion in enterprise value. Nvidia previously invested $2 billion in each company, strengthening its relationships with suppliers involved in optical networking and data-centre connectivity. While the deal reinforces Nvidia’s strategic influence, its enormous size also highlights the capital requirements and financing risks associated with expanding the infrastructure supporting advanced computing. NVIDIA shares lost momentum early in September after failing to break decisively above the $236 resistance zone, with the rejection sending the stock back below $210 but we have seen a decent rebound recently. Shares have climbed above $233 today as investors responded positively to expanding infrastructure partnerships and CEO projections, but buyers are not able to sustain the rally above $243 and we saw dive to $200 again last week but we saw some improvement yesterday as NVDA finds support at the 50 weekly SMA. However we’re back at the 50 SMA today. Despite growing concerns, demand for computing capacity remains substantial. Reports indicate that Anthropic plans to increase its computing capacity beyond 3.5 gigawatts by the end of 2026, potentially reaching approximately 7 gigawatts in 2027. Such expansion highlights the enormous infrastructure requirements associated with developing and operating increasingly sophisticated models, providing continued support for Nvidia’s longer-term growth prospects. Samsung Electronics is also reportedly preparing to manufacture base dies for high-bandwidth memory chips intended for Nvidia and AMD at its second foundry facility in Taylor, Texas. Construction is expected to begin this month, with mass production targeted for 2030. Competition is another growing concern. Google and Oracle have announced plans to make Google’s Tensor Processing Units (TPUs) available through Oracle Cloud Infrastructure from 2027. This gives customers another option beyond Nvidia-powered systems, as major technology companies increasingly look to develop custom processors to reduce computing costs and dependence on external suppliers. Nvidia retains considerable advantages through its established software ecosystem, performance and customer relationships. However, expanding competition could eventually put pressure on pricing and market share, even if overall computing demand continues growing. ASML reported record third-quarter sales of €11.7 billion but warned that semiconductor manufacturing capacity planned for 2027 and 2028 might not fully satisfy anticipated demand. The company forecast fourth-quarter revenue of €14.2 billion to €15.2 billion and narrowed its 2026 sales guidance to €44 billion–€45 billion. Although manufacturing constraints could support semiconductor pricing, they could also delay production expansion and complicate Nvidia’s supply arrangements. Financing is another concern. CoreWeave has experienced pressure as yields on its $1.25 billion bond issue due in 2032 reportedly climbed towards 15%. Such borrowing costs highlight the risks facing companies investing heavily in data-centre infrastructure. Electricity shortages are also creating deployment problems. Amazon reportedly has Nvidia-equipped server racks waiting in warehouses because some facilities lack sufficient electricity to operate them. Delays could increase storage costs and postpone revenue generation from infrastructure investments. Nvidia continues to benefit from substantial long-term computing demand, expanding customer relationships and its dominant position in advanced processors. However, the market is increasingly questioning whether infrastructure investment can maintain its previous growth trajectory. The Democratic midterm victories introduce another layer of uncertainty, with potential restrictions on data-centre construction adding to concerns about financing, electricity availability and competition. Technically, $200 is the immediate support level to watch. A sustained break below it could expose $180, while a recovery above $210 would provide an initial indication that buyers are regaining control. For now, the balance of risks has shifted towards sellers. Nvidia’s longer-term growth prospects remain significant, but investors may become less willing to pay premium valuations if political resistance and infrastructure costs begin threatening the expansion plans underpinning semiconductor earnings.

title: Where Could NVIDIA’s Next Growth Come From? - Trefis
content: For questions about this article or underlying research, email help@trefis.com. NVIDIA (NVDA) reported revenue of $96.2 billion in fiscal Q2 2027, up 105.9% from a year earlier. Management expects revenue to grow about 70% in fiscal 2028, and said supply constraints limit that forecast. During the August 26, 2026 call detailing these projections, management said NVIDIA had just begun shipping a new generation of data center hardware. What is that hardware, and are customers buying it yet? The new hardware is Vera Rubin, and customers placed orders before the first units left. Management said production shipments began in August 2026. By then, NVIDIA already had purchase orders from every major AI cloud and system maker, along with every major hyperscaler, as the largest cloud companies are known. Management expects Vera Rubin to be the fastest product ramp in NVIDIA’s history, which is a forecast, not a result. Vera Rubin operates as a whole system rather than a single chip. The architecture spans the Vera CPU, the Rubin GPU, networking equipment and the Groq LPU. For every gigawatt of AI data center capacity built with Vera Rubin, management puts NVIDIA’s revenue opportunity at $40 billion. That compares with $25 billion for Blackwell, the generation before it. Management also named one large buyer. AWS is deploying an additional 2 million NVIDIA GPUs from fiscal Q3 2027 through fiscal Q2 2029, alongside Vera CPUs, some of them integrated with Rubin. How Much Of NVIDIA’s Business Could Vera Rubin Become? Management said Vera Rubin is expected to make up about 20% of NVIDIA’s data center revenue in fiscal Q3 2027, its first quarter of shipments. That represents a fifth of the business driving most of NVIDIA’s sales. Data center revenue reached $89 billion in fiscal Q2 2027, up 18% from the previous quarter. For fiscal Q3 2027 as a whole, management expects total sales of $108 billion, plus or minus 2%. NVIDIA’s next earnings report is due on November 17, 2026. Vera Rubin is not a side product at a large company. It serves as the next version of the hardware NVIDIA already sells most of, and NVIDIA’s Compute & Networking segment made up 89.6% of company revenue in fiscal 2026. The share price has not kept pace with the sales. NVIDIA stock ended November 3, 2026, trading 13.6% below its highest close of the past year, set on October 6. Over the year to November 3, the stock returned 2.3%, compared with 11.9% for the S&P 500. At 25.9 times trailing earnings, against 22.8 for the S&P 500, the stock trades at only a small premium to the market, which suggests investors expect NVIDIA’s growth to slow well below the 83.4% revenue growth of the past twelve months. Supply could. Management expects supply to remain a bottleneck at least through the end of fiscal 2028, meaning NVIDIA’s sales are limited by what it can get made, not by orders alone. Costs are rising too. Memory prices have climbed more than management expected, and management now sees gross margin bottoming at 71% to 72% in fiscal Q4 2027. Management expects margins to settle at 72% to 73% in fiscal 2028, once price increases it has already put through take effect. Then there is the question of who pays for the hardware. NVIDIA has invested nearly $50 billion in frontier AI labs, and plans to back some of their purchases with its own balance sheet. Management expects demand from those labs to make up roughly a quarter of its business in fiscal 2028, and said on the call that some will call this circular financing. Vera Rubin’s share of data center revenue, measured against management’s guide, is the number to watch in NVIDIA’s next earnings report. content: Nvidia stock recovered approximately 3% after retreating toward $200, as improving geopolitical sentiment supports technology stocks, while Big Tech earnings, rising infrastructure costs, custom-chip competition and financing risks continue to challenge the semiconductor sector Nvidia (NASDAQ: NVDA) shares have struggled to maintain their upward momentum after retreating from record highs above $243, falling toward $200 as disappointing Big Tech earnings and concerns about infrastructure spending weighed on semiconductor stocks. The stock recently recovered toward $220 after finding support around $210, but the rebound lost momentum as investors reassessed the sustainability of technology companies’ enormous infrastructure commitments. Nvidia is now attempting another recovery, gaining approximately 3% as improving sentiment surrounding the Middle East conflict supports broader market sentiment. Comments from President Trump during a Fox News interview concerning Israel and the conflict with Iran have encouraged expectations that Washington could pursue a diplomatic agreement with Tehran. The prospect of de-escalation has also contributed to downward pressure on oil prices, helping improve sentiment across financial markets. However, the broader semiconductor outlook remains complicated. Strong demand for processors and memory does not necessarily guarantee continued earnings growth, particularly when customers must secure financing, electricity and operational capacity to deploy increasingly expensive computing infrastructure. Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang’s reported involvement in Marvell Technology’s acquisition of Lumentum Holdings has highlighted Nvidia’s growing influence across the semiconductor supply chain. According to Bloomberg, Marvell CEO Matthew Murphy and Lumentum CEO Michael Hurlston consulted Huang before announcing the transaction, which values Lumentum at an enterprise value of approximately $115 billion. Nvidia previously invested $2 billion in each company, strengthening its financial relationships with suppliers involved in optical networking and data-centre connectivity. The development highlights how Nvidia is expanding its influence beyond processors, although the enormous transaction also raises questions about financing, integration and the capital required to expand infrastructure. Nvidia has received additional support from reports that Anthropic plans to significantly expand its computing capacity. According to a New York Times report, the company expects capacity to exceed 3.5 gigawatts by the end of 2026, with plans to increase that figure to approximately 7 gigawatts in 2027. Such expansion highlights the substantial computing requirements associated with developing and operating increasingly sophisticated models. Meanwhile, Samsung Electronics reportedly plans to manufacture base dies for high-bandwidth memory (HBM) chips destined for Nvidia and AMD at its second foundry facility in Taylor, Texas. Construction is expected to begin this month, with mass production targeted for 2030. NVIDIA shares lost momentum early in September after failing to break decisively above the $236 resistance zone, with the rejection sending the stock back below $210 but we have seen a decent rebound recently. Shares have climbed above $233 today as investors responded positively to expanding infrastructure partnerships and CEO projections, but buyers are not able to sustain the rally above $243 and we saw dive to $200 again last week but we’re seeing some improvement today as NVDA finds support at the 50 weekly SMA. Competition is another concern for Nvidia. Google and Oracle recently announced plans to make Google’s Tensor Processing Units (TPUs) available through Oracle Cloud Infrastructure from 2027. This marks an important development because Google’s custom processors will become accessible through another major cloud platform, giving customers additional alternatives to Nvidia-powered systems.
